prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its active form, which made possible incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: I keep a single-achievement B001 prize to Holst, Drucker and Mojsov, and my reasons are scientific. The round-1 exchange showed that all six of us rest the case on the same arc: proglucagon processing, the truncated active GLP-1(7-36) amide, human incretin physiology with insulinotropic, glucagonostatic and satiety actions, receptor-level mechanism, and then outcome trials showing glycaemic, weight, cardiovascular and renal benefit. The mechanism is understood end to end and has been confirmed independently for two decades, so the work is mature. No other shortlisted candidate combines that much original physiology with that much demonstrated benefit to patients. The citation I propose is physiology-led and names the therapeutic consequence, so it does not claim to credit the drug engineering. After round 1 I am more confident of that framing, because no member proposed a different B001 laureate set and no member argued the work is premature.
statement.case_against: The weakness is still credit, and round 1 did not remove it. A physiology-led trio omits Lotte Bjerre Knudsen, whose acylation chemistry produced the long-acting analogues that reached patients, and it can be read as honouring the hormone and not the drug. Mojsov's priority for the active peptide relative to Habener's group, who are not among the credited names, is contested, and no member, including me, has cited a document that settles it. I rely on general knowledge there. If the committee cannot defend Mojsov by the end of this round, my fallback would be a Holst, Drucker and Knudsen configuration with a citation that moves toward the therapeutic arm. That would be a substantive change to the achievement, not a wording change. I would not name a trio I could not defend publicly just because the opening ranks were unanimous.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius argues that engineering a native peptide with a half-life of minutes into a once-weekly drug is a scientific achievement and not routine development, that she excludes Knudsen only because three places force a choice, and that she would hesitate most over Mojsov if colleagues think the therapeutic arm carries the prize.
responses.response: I accept the first point and it changes how I state my case. In round 1 I treated Knudsen's exclusion mainly as a risk to the citation. I now think it is a real scientific omission, and the committee should say so openly. I do not agree that Mojsov is the natural name to drop, though. The identification and synthesis of the active GLP-1(7-36) amide is what made a drug target of a peptide that was previously a precursor fragment, and removing that step breaks the arc more than removing a later optimisation. If the arc has to be cut, I would drop the discoverer whose step is least separable from others' work. That judgement needs the priority record, which none of us has cited. Until we have it, I keep Holst, Drucker and Mojsov and say plainly that this leaves out the drug-engineering step.

responses.point: Linnarsson says he would not dismiss Knudsen as merely industrial, because Nobel recognition has honoured translational steps that were conceptually new. He still lands on the basic trio because the citation can say the physiology enabled the therapy and because Mojsov's identification of the active form is closer to discovery than formulation. He also keeps B017 and B012 as alternatives, and rates B012 harder to defend as fair than B001.
responses.response: I agree with most of this, and my preferred configuration is the same as his. The point I take most seriously is that the Knudsen question is about precedent as well as fairness: if the committee honours a conceptually new translational step here, it should say why long-acting acylation counts when other drug-development steps would not. I do not think the shortlist gives me enough to make that case today, so I stay with discovery. On B012 I partly revise my round-1 view. I proposed Nagel, Hegemann and Deisseroth as defensible, but his argument that Bamberg's channel electrophysiology, Boyden's neuronal deployment and Miesenboeck's earlier concept are each necessary steps is stronger than my reply allowed. I still keep B012 as an alternative on merit, but I now regard it as the harder of the two alternatives to allocate fairly, and I would not put it forward without a stated principle for the cut.

responses.point: Sandberg comes down on the discovery side because the long-acting analogues depend on the physiology and on identification of the active peptide, and he says an industrial medicinal-chemistry achievement is hard to credit to one person under a three-person cap. He also ranks B051 second and B017 third, with a two-person CAR-T credit of June and Sadelain.
responses.response: The cap argument is the strongest of his points, and it is why I stay with the discovery trio. I would qualify it, though. Acylation for long-acting analogues is credited to Knudsen as an individual in the candidate, so the credit is not diffuse in the way he suggests, and I would rather concede that we are leaving out a named person than say the credit cannot be assigned. On B051 I still see Walter and Mori as a clean pair and the mechanism as conceptually original. My reservation is the one he has already named: translation to disease is early, and the PERK arm lies outside the credit. As a basic-science alternative it is stronger than B012 on attribution, but I keep B017 and B012 ahead because their effects on patients or on experimental physiology are already demonstrated. On his June and Sadelain pairing for B017, I think the cut is defensible but it leaves out a contributor to the engineered-T-cell lineage, so I would not claim it is clean.

responses.point: The chair would hold B012 for a later year unless the committee can agree a rule for cutting six names to three. He also says that Rosenberg's adoptive transfer and early engineered-T-cell trials are part of the CAR-T lineage, and that B001 meets the criterion of benefit to humankind in a way B051 and B050 do not yet.
responses.response: I accept his rule requirement for B012, and as a circuit neuroscientist I have to admit that I cannot give one that I would defend. A channel-discovery rule would favour Nagel and Hegemann. A neuronal-deployment rule would favour Deisseroth and Boyden. Neither is clearly correct, so I now agree that B012 should wait unless the committee agrees a principle, and I treat it as an alternative only. This also means B017 is the better fallback if B001 stalls on credit. On Rosenberg I partly side with him: the adoptive transfer and early trial work belong to the lineage, but Perlmann and Wahren-Herlenius are right that it does not map cleanly onto the CAR design itself. If B017 became the fallback, I would want the committee to decide explicitly whether the prize honours the engineered receptor or the broader cell-therapy lineage, and to say how the question of Eshhar is handled.

responses.point: Perlmann says he would not crown a method while knowingly leaving out half the discovery chain, and that the tool-versus-discovery question for optogenetics remains open. He also treats the omission of Habener from the GLP-1 credit as part of the discussion of Mojsov's priority.
responses.response: His caution on B012 persuades me further than it did in round 1. On the tool-versus-discovery point I would add that, for a Physiology or Medicine prize, optogenetics is strongest as a causal tool that let investigators test how circuits drive behaviour, and in my own field that is decisive, but I cannot show that it has changed disease care. That gap is more tolerable for a prize in physiology than he implies, but it does not solve the allocation problem. On Habener I agree he belongs in the priority discussion. The honest position is that the committee has not cited a record that distinguishes Habener's group from Mojsov on the active peptide, and I would not claim to resolve that from memory. If the committee decides that the record leaves joint priority, the question becomes whether Mojsov or the group is the better credit under the cap, and that would need a source we have not yet been given.

uncertainties: How the priority for identifying and synthesising the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide divides between Mojsov and Habener's group, which I cannot settle from documents available to the committee. This decides whether Mojsov is named without reservation.

Whether a physiology-led trio can be defended publicly while leaving out Knudsen, and whether the committee would accept a Holst, Drucker and Knudsen configuration if Mojsov's priority is judged too unclear.
For B017, whether Rosenberg and Eshhar belong in the credited set, and so whether it is the more defensible fallback than B012.
For B012, whether any principle for cutting six names to three can be defended. I do not have one.
Whether a two-part prize would dilute the GLP-1 credit. I currently judge that it would, but I have not seen a pairing that is cleanly attributed and of comparable scale.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for the preferred configuration or the listed alternatives. I work on motor circuits in zebrafish and lamprey, and optogenetics (B012) is a tool in that field, so I treat that as subject expertise and not an institutional tie; B012 is not in my preferred configuration. I co-authored with Thomas Perlmann in 2009 on dopamine neurons derived from stem cells, and with Sten Grillner and Patrik Ernfors on other work. None of these three is a credited candidate. My disclosures are unchanged since round 1.
